slides.title: Deadlock & System Model
slides.body: Deadlock & System Model

slides.title: What Is a Deadlock?
slides.body:
Processes Stuck Waiting Forever
A set of processes is in a deadlock state 
When every process in the set is waiting for an event that can be caused only by another process in the same set
slides.notes: Alright, let's understand what a deadlock is. Imagine multiple processes are waiting for resources, but none of them can continue because each one is waiting for another process to release something. This creates a situation where everyone keeps waiting indefinitely, and no process is able to make progress.

slides.title: What Is a Deadlock?
slides.body:
Processes Stuck Waiting Forever
In an operating system, that "event" is almost always the release of a resource
Each deadlocked process is holding at least one resource and is waiting to acquire a resource currently held by another process in the set
Resource 1
Resource 2
slides.notes: Moving on, let's see why deadlocks occur in an operating system. Here, the event each process is waiting for is usually the release of a resource. Notice that every process already holds one resource but is waiting for another resource that's currently held by another process. Since no process releases its resource, they all remain blocked, creating a deadlock situation.

slides.title: What Is a Deadlock?
slides.body:
Processes Stuck Waiting Forever
Since no process will give up what it holds until its own request is granted, the waiting is circular and can never resolve on its own
slides.notes: Now, let's understand why this situation cannot resolve automatically. Each process continues to hold its allocated resource until it gets the one it's waiting for. As a result, every process ends up waiting on another process in a circular chain. Since no one releases its resource first, the cycle continues forever, and the deadlock persists.

slides.title: Deadlock?
slides.body:
It involves a set of processes — never a single process alone
Each process holds at least one resource and waits for another held within the set
The dependency is circular — the waiting forms a closed loop
The wait is permanent — only outside intervention (killing or preempting a process) can break it, so throughput for those processes drops to zero
Processes Block Each Other
slides.notes: Moving on, a deadlock always involves a group of processes rather than a single process. In this situation, every process is holding a resource while waiting for another one within the same group. This creates a circular dependency, so none of the processes can continue. As a result, the deadlock remains until an external action, such as terminating or preempting a process, breaks the cycle.

slides.title: System Model for Deadlocks
slides.body:
Processes & Resources
To reason about deadlock precisely, the OS is modelled as a collection of resource types:
A request for a type can be satisfied by any one of its instances
 Where each type has a fixed number of identical instances
R1
R2
R3
slides.notes: Now, before we understand how deadlocks occur, let's look at the system model. Here, the operating system is viewed as a collection of different resource types. Each resource type has a fixed number of identical instances, and whenever a process requests a resource, it can be allocated any available instance of that particular resource type.

slides.title: Processes, Resources & the Request Cycle
slides.body:
Example
A system with three identical printers has one resource type with three instances, and a process needing "a printer" is happy with any of them
Printer 1
Printer 2
Printer 3
slides.notes: Moving on, let's understand this with an example. Consider a system that has three identical printers. Here, printers form a single resource type with three instances. So, when a process requests a printer, it doesn't require a specific one—it can use any available printer instance.

slides.title: System Model for Deadlocks
slides.body:
Processes, Resources & Request Cycle
The important one is request: if the resource is not free, the requesting process blocks and waits until an instance becomes available
Allocation itself is not a process step — it is the internal action the OS performs to grant an instance, i.e. the successful transition out of the request state
Request
Use
Release
A process uses a resource in three steps
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the resource usage cycle. Every process follows three steps: it first requests a resource, then uses it, and finally releases it. The request step is the most importantbecause if the required resource isn't available, the process is blocked until an instance becomes free. Once that happens, the operating system allocates the resource, allowing the process to continue.

slides.title: Resource Lifecycle
slides.body:
Three-Step Cycle
A Type groups identical resources; any free instance satisfies a request
Request
The process asks the OS; if nothing is free, it blocks
Use
The process operates on the granted resource
Release
The process returns the resource so others can use it
slides.notes: Moving on, let's summarize the resource lifecycle. A resource type represents a group of identical resources, so any available instance can satisfy a request. A process first requests a resource, and if none is available, it waits. Once the resource is granted, the process uses it and finally releases it, making it available for other processes.

slides.title: System Model for Deadlocks
slides.body: Resource Types & Instances
slides.notes: Now, let's put these steps together. A process begins by requesting a resource from the operating system. If no instance is available, it waits until one is allocated. After receiving the resource, the process performs its task using it. Once the work is complete, the process releases the resource back to the operating system so it can be assigned to another process.
tables: Process asks the OS for a resource; blocks if none is free. The OS allocates a free instance to complete this step
Process returns the resource to the OS

slides.title: Preemption
slides.body:
Resources are also classified by whether they can be taken back:
Preemptable
Can be safely taken from a process and restored later
CPU state is saved, and memory is swapped to disk if needed, so these rarely cause deadlock
Non-Preemptable
Cannot be taken without causing failure (printer, lock, tape drive)
Deadlock problems center on these
Resource Classification
slides.notes: Moving on, resources can also be classified based on whether the operating system can take them back. Some resources are preemptable, meaning they can be safely reclaimed and restored later, so they rarely lead to deadlocks. Others are non-preemptable and cannot be taken away without causing a failure. Since these resources must be released by the process itself, deadlocks mainly occur with them.

slides.title: Resource Usage Cycle
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Finally, think of resource management like borrowing a library book. You first request the book, then use it, and finally return it so someone else can borrow it. Operating systems manage resources in the same way, ensuring that shared resources are requested, used, and released in an orderly manner.

slides.body: Necessary Conditions

slides.title: Four Conditions for Deadlock
slides.body:
All Must Hold Together
Deadlock is not random — it can occur only when four specific conditions all hold at the same time These are known as the Coffman conditions
Mutual Exclusion
Hold-and-Wait
No Preemption
Circular Wait
slides.notes: Now, let's move to the conditions required for a deadlock. A deadlock doesn't happen by chance. It occurs only when four conditions exist together at the same time. These are called the Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold-and-Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. In the next few slides, we'll understand each of these conditions one by one.

slides.title: Four Conditions for Deadlock
slides.body:
All Must Hold Together
The practical importance is this: 
if we can guarantee even one of them never holds, deadlock becomes impossible
Mutual Exclusion
A resource is held by only one process at a time
Hold-and-Wait
A process holds one resource while waiting for another
No Preemption
A resource cannot be forcibly taken back
Circular Wait
A closed chain of processes each waits for the next
slides.notes: these four conditions together determine whether a deadlock can occur., The conditions are Mutual Exclusion, where a resource is used by only one process at a time; Hold-and-Wait, where a process keeps one resource while requesting another; No Preemption, where the operating system cannot forcibly reclaim a resource; and Circular Wait, where the waiting forms a closed loop among processes

slides.title: Four Conditions for Deadlock
slides.body: All Must Hold Together

slides.title: Deadlock
slides.body:
Four Conditions
The first three conditions describe how a single process behaves with resources; 
The fourth describes a relationship across several processes
Circular Wait
slides.notes: there's an important distinction to notice here. The first three conditions—Mutual Exclusion, Hold-and-Wait, and No Preemption—describe how an individual process interacts with resources. Circular Wait is different because it involves multiple processes and the dependency that forms between them.

slides.title: Deadlock
slides.body:
Mutual Exclusion
At least one resource must be non-sharable, usable by only one process at a time
A printer is non-sharable; a read-only file is sharable, and sharable resources never cause deadlock
Hold-and-Wait
A process is holding at least one resource while requesting more
If a process always obtained everything it needed at once, it could never sit holding one resource and waiting for another
Four Conditions
slides.notes: Now, let's understand the first two conditions. Mutual Exclusion means the resource must be one that cannot be shared, so only a single process can use it at a time. That's why a printer can contribute to a deadlock, whereas a read-only file cannot. Hold-and-Wait means a process doesn't release the resource it already has while requesting another one. If it received all the required resources together, this situation would never arise.

slides.title: Deadlock
slides.body:
No Preemption
A resource cannot be forcibly taken from a process; it is released only voluntarily when the process finishes
A half-completed print job cannot be snatched away mid-print.
Circular Wait
There is a set {P0, P1, …, Pn} where P0 waits for a resource held by P1, P1 waits for one held by P2, …, and Pn waits for one held by P0 — a closed loop of dependencies
Four Conditions
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the remaining two conditions. No Preemption means once a process has a resource, the operating system cannot take it back forcefully; the process must release it on its own after completing its work. Circular Wait occurs when multiple processes end up waiting on one another in a closed loop, with each process depending on the next, causing none of them to proceed.

slides.title: Deadlock
slides.body:
All four must hold at the same time for deadlock to be possible — which is exactly why breaking any single one (the basis of prevention) makes deadlock impossible
Four Conditions

Print job cannot be pulled mid-print
A closed loop of waiting processes
P0 waits P1, P1 waits P2, Pn waits P0

slides.notes:
Mutual Exclusion — one meeting room, one team at a time.
Hold-and-Wait — holding the mixing bowl while waiting for the oven.
No Preemption — a car can't be pulled out mid car-wash.
Circular Wait - a loop of people each needing what the next one is holding, so no one can start.

slides.title: Three Problems Often Confused
slides.body: Same Symptom, Different Cause
slides.notes: Now, before moving ahead, let's distinguish between three terms that are often confused because they appear similar. Although all of them affect progress, the reason is different in each case. In Deadlock, all the involved processes are blocked permanently. In Starvation, the system continues to run, but one process keeps waiting. In Livelock, processes remain active and keep responding to one another, yet no useful work gets completed.

slides.title: Modeling Deadlock with a Graph
slides.body:
Resource Allocation Graph (RAG)
The four conditions are easier to reason about as a picture than as words
A Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) draws the request-allocate relationships directly, showing who wants what and who holds what
slides.notes: Moving on, instead of understanding deadlock only through definitions, we can represent it visually using a Resource Allocation Graph, or RAG. This graph captures the relationship between processes and resources by showing which resources are allocated and which ones are being requested, making it much easier to analyze deadlock situations.

slides.title: Modeling Deadlock with a Graph
slides.body: Resource Allocation Graph (RAG)
slides.notes: Next, to read a Resource Allocation Graph correctly, we need to understand its two edge types. A request edge starts from a process and points to a resource type, showing that the process is waiting for any available instance of that resource. An assignment edge goes from a specific resource instance to a process, indicating that the operating system has already allocated that instance to the process.
tables: Process wants any instance of this type
A specific instance is already given to the process

Processes, Resources & Edges
slides.notes: There are two types of edges. A request edge goes from a process to a resource, showing that the process is waiting for that resource. An assignment edge goes from a resource to a process, indicating that the resource has already been allocated to that process. These edges help us visualize resource allocation and identify possible deadlocks.

slides.title: Resource Allocation Graph
slides.body:
Request edge
Points from the process circle to the resource square as a whole (the outer container), because the process wants any instance of the type, not a specific one
Assignment edge
Starts from a specific dot inside the square and points to the process circle, showing that one particular instance has been claimed
Requests & Assignments
slides.notes: Now, let's understand how these edges are drawn in a Resource Allocation Graph. A request edge connects a process to the resource type itself because the process is simply asking for any available instance. In contrast, an assignment edge begins from a particular resource instance and points to the process, indicating that this specific instance has already been allocated.

slides.title: Resource Allocation Graph
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: Finally, think of a Resource Allocation Graph like an office where colleagues share stationery. If an arrow goes from a person to a stapler, it means, "I want to use the stapler." If the arrow goes from the stapler to the person, it means, "I already have the stapler." This simple analogy makes it easier to understand how request and assignment edges represent resource usage in an operating system.

slides.title: Finding Deadlocks
slides.body:
Cycle Detection
Once the graph is drawn, deadlock detection becomes a search for cycles
But a cycle means different things depending on whether the resources involved have a single instance or many
slides.notes: once the Resource Allocation Graph is ready, detecting a deadlock comes down to checking for cycles in the graph. However, it's important to note that the meaning of a cycle depends on the type of resources involved. Whether the resources have a single instance or multiple instances changes how that cycle is interpreted, which we'll discuss next.

slides.title: Detecting Deadlock via Cycles
slides.body:
Deadlock or Not?
A cycle
Is a closed loop of arrows in the graph.
Single-instance resources
A cycle always means deadlock
Multiple-instance resources
A cycle is necessary but not sufficient
No cycle
Guarantees no deadlock
slides.notes: Next, let's see how to interpret the cycles we find in a Resource Allocation Graph. A cycle is simply a closed loop formed by the arrows in the graph. If every resource in that cycle has only a single instance, then the cycle itself confirms a deadlock. However, when resources have multiple instances, a cycle alone does not guarantee a deadlock—it only indicates that one might exist. On the other hand, if the graph contains no cycle, we can conclude that there is no deadlock.

slides.title: Handling Deadlocks
slides.body: Handling Deadlocks

slides.title: Handling Deadlocks
slides.body:
Four Strategies
Detecting deadlock is only half the story — the OS needs a policy for dealing with it. There are four broad strategies, differing in when they act and how much they cost
Prevention
Avoidance
Detection & Recovery
Ignore (Ostrich Algorithm)
slides.notes: Now, identifying a deadlock is only part of the solution. The operating system also needs a strategy to handle it, and these strategies mainly differ in when they take action and the cost involved. Broadly, there are four approaches: Prevention,avoidance, Detection & Recovery , Ignore(ostrich algorithm)

slides.title: Handling Deadlocks
slides.body:
Prevention
Design the system so that at least one of the four necessary conditions can never hold. A structural, build-time guarantee
Avoidance
At run time, use advance information about each process's maximum needs to grant a request only if the system stays in a "safe state" (the Banker's Algorithm)
Four Strategies
slides.notes: Prevention takes a proactive approach by designing the system in such a way that at least one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock can never occur, making deadlock impossible by design. Avoidance, on the other hand, makes decisions at run time. Before granting a resource request, the operating system checks whether doing so keeps the system in a safe state using information about each process's maximum resource requirements. We'll study the Banker's Algorithm, which follows this approach, in the next session.

slides.title: Handling Deadlocks
slides.body:
Detection & Recovery
Allow deadlock to occur, run a detection algorithm periodically, then recover by aborting processes or preempting their resources 
Ignore (Ostrich Algorithm)
Assume deadlock is so rare that it is cheaper to do nothing and simply restart if the system hangs
Four Strategies
slides.notes: In Detection and Recovery, the operating system allows deadlocks to happen, periodically checks whether one has occurred, and then recovers by either terminating the affected processes or taking back their resources. The final approach is Ignore, also called the Ostrich Algorithm, where the operating system assumes deadlocks are extremely rare and chooses not to handle them, simply restarting the system if it eventually becomes unresponsive.

slides.title: Handling Deadlocks - Four Strategies
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A hospital can vaccinate to prevent disease, screen for early symptoms, treat after diagnosis, or ignore a rare condition.Similarly, an operating system can prevent deadlocks, avoid them through safety checks, detect and recover after they occur, or ignore them if they are extremely uncommon.

slides.title: Strategy Comparison & Trade-offs
slides.body:
Overhead vs Safety vs Practicality
 Prevention is cheap on CPU but wastes resources; avoidance is the reverse.
The four strategies trade overhead against the strength of the guarantee — but "overhead" comes in two forms: 
CPU cost at run time, and 
Resource waste from holding or restricting resources
slides.notes: Finally, each deadlock-handling strategy involves a trade-off between system safety and the overhead it introduces. Here, overhead refers to both the CPU time spent making decisions and the resource utilization caused by holding or restricting resources. For example, Prevention requires very little run-time CPU effort but may leave resources underutilized, whereas Avoidance uses resources more efficiently but incurs additional run-time computation to ensure the system always remains in a safe state.

slides.title: Deadlock Prevention
slides.body: Deadlock Prevention

slides.title: Breaking the First Two Conditions
slides.body:
Deadlock Prevention
Prevention works by designing the system so that one of the four conditions can never hold. We take them two at a time, with the technique and the reasoning for each
slides.notes:
Moving on, let's now look at how deadlock prevention works in practice.
 The main idea is to design the system so that at least one of the four necessary conditions 
for deadlock can never exist. We'll examine these conditions one by one, starting with the first two, 
and understand the technique used to break each condition along with the reasoning behind it.

slides.title: Deadlock Prevention
slides.body:
Attacking Mutual Exclusion
Make resources sharable 
Sharable resources (e.g., read-only files) never need mutual exclusion, so they can never be part of a deadlock
Spooling
Instead of giving a process the printer directly, all output is written to a shared spool queue that the printer daemon drains. The printer becomes sharable
Limitation
Many resources are inherently non-sharable (a process truly writing to a device), and the spool space itself is finite and can fill up, so mutual exclusion usually cannot be removed entirely
slides.notes: Now, let's see how to break the Mutual Exclusion condition. The idea is to make resources sharable whenever possible. For example, read-only files can be accessed by multiple processes simultaneously, so they cannot cause deadlocks. Another approach is spooling, where print requests are placed in a shared queue instead of giving the printer directly to a process. However, many resources are inherently non-sharable, and spool space is limited, so this condition cannot always be eliminated.

slides.title: Deadlock Prevention
slides.body:
Attacking Hold-and-Wait 
Request everything up front
a process must acquire all the resources it will ever need before it starts, so it never holds some while waiting for others
Release-before-request
a process may request new resources only when it holds none; it must release everything first
Drawbacks
low resource utilization (resources are held long before they are actually used) and possible starvation (a process needing several popular resources may wait indefinitely)
slides.notes: Next, another way to prevent deadlocks is by eliminating the Hold-and-Wait condition. This can be done either by making a process collect all the resources it needs before it begins execution, or by requiring it to release its current resources before asking for new ones. While these approaches prevent a process from waiting while holding resources, they also reduce resource utilization and may cause some processes to wait for a long time before getting everything they need

slides.title: Deadlock Prevention : Eliminating Hold-and-Wait
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: An exam invigilator makes every student collect all their stationery before the exam starts, not one item at a time.

slides.title: Deadlock Prevention
slides.body:
Forced Release & Resource Ordering
The remaining two conditions are attacked by reclaiming resources when a process would otherwise block, and by imposing a fixed order on how resources may be requested
slides.notes: Moving on, the remaining two conditions are handled using different approaches. One approach forces a process to release its resources if it would otherwise get blocked, while the other enforces a fixed order for requesting resources. Both techniques are designed to prevent the remaining deadlock conditions from occurring.

slides.title: Forced Release & Resource Ordering
slides.body:
Attacking No Preemption
Ignore (Ostrich Algorithm)
If a process holding some resources requests another that cannot be granted immediately, all of its currently-held resources are preempted (released)
Restart
The process is restarted only when it can regain its old resources plus the new one it wanted
Where it applies?
Only to resources whose state can be easily saved and restored, such as CPU registers or memory — not to a printer mid-job
slides.notes: Now, another way to prevent deadlock is to allow resources to be taken back instead of letting a process wait indefinitely. So, if a process can't get the next resource it needs, the operating system asks it to give up the resources it's already holding and lets it try again later. This approach is practical only for resources whose state can be saved and restored easily, such as CPU registers or memory, but not for devices like a printer that's already in the middle of a task.

slides.title: Forced Release & Resource Ordering
slides.body:
Attacking Circular Wait 
Assign an ordering
Give every resource type a unique number F(R1), F(R2), …
The rule
A process may request resources only in increasing order: after requesting Ri, it may request Rj only if F(Rj) > F(Ri)
Why it works?
A circular wait would require some resource to be both lower and higher in the ordering than another, which is impossible, so no loop can ever form
slides.notes: Finally, the Circular Wait condition is prevented by introducing a fixed order for all resource types. Once this ordering is defined, every process must follow the same sequence while requesting resources and cannot go back to a lower-ordered resource after acquiring a higher one. Since every process follows a single direction in the ordering, a circular chain of waiting can never be formed, which eliminates the possibility of a deadlock.

slides.title: Forced Release & Resource Ordering
slides.body:
Real-World Example
Two threads deadlock when they take two locks in opposite order
Thread A does lock(X) then lock(Y)
while Thread B does lock(Y) then lock(X)
If A holds X and B holds Y, each waits forever
The fix is exactly this ordering rule: every thread acquires locks in the same global order
slides.notes: Now, let's connect this idea to a real-world scenario. Imagine two threads that both need two locks, but they acquire them in different orders. One thread takes X before Y, while the other takes Y before X. If each thread gets its first lock, both end up waiting for the other, resulting in a deadlock. The solution is simple—every thread follows the same predefined lock order, ensuring this situation never arises.

slides.title: Prevention Comes at a Cost
slides.body:
Safety Versus Utilization
Every prevention technique buys a deadlock-free guarantee at the cost of some flexibility or resource utilization
slides.notes: Moving on, while deadlock prevention guarantees that deadlocks cannot occur, that guarantee comes with a trade-off. By restricting how resources are requested or used, the system loses some flexibility and may not utilize resources as efficiently.

slides.title: Prevention Comes at a Cost
slides.body:
Safety Versus Utilization
Prevention guarantees no deadlock, but often reduces concurrency and resource utilization
slides.notes: Finally, HERE WE HAVE  the trade-offs of each prevention technique. Every method successfully eliminates one of the necessary deadlock conditions, but each introduces its own limitation. |Whether it's limited sharing, reduced resource utilization, the overhead of saving and restoring state, or the need for a strict resource ordering, every guarantee comes at a cost. The key takeaway is that deadlock prevention completely avoids deadlocks, but often sacrifices concurrency and efficient resource utilization.

slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A housing society that locks every gate to stop intruders also slows down its own residents entering daily.
